                                               PROJECT NO. 58482

LARGE LOAD DEMAND                                            §                 PUBLIC UTILITY
MANAGEMENT SERVICE                                           §                 COMMISSION OF TEXAS

COMMENTS OF FEDOR MIKHEEV ON THE PROPOSED NEW 16 TAC § 25.521

Fedor Mikheev files these comments on the proposal for publication of new 16 Texas Administrative
Code § 25.521, approved by the Commission at its July 30, 2026 open meeting. These comments arise
from graduate research conducted at the Texas A&M University Energy Institute, presently under peer
review in the marine affairs and policy section of a peer-reviewed ocean and coastal policy journal. I file
in my individual capacity.
I bring twenty years of operational, technical and commercial experience with major international energy
service companies, advancing from application engineering through district and country leadership,
accountable for service delivery, capital equipment programs and the operating commitments made to
petrochemical, refining and upstream customers across several regions. That work was concerned
throughout with how industrial facilities are optimized in practice: what a plant is solving for when it
schedules production, where its electrical flexibility resides as against where a model would assume it
resides, and what it costs an operator to give any of it up. I am lead author of a study of multi-utility
coordination in the Port Houston Baytown-La Porte corridor, and filed comments of record in this project
on July 16, 2026 (Item No. 28).
These comments supersede my July 16 filing to the extent of any inconsistency. I have also filed
comments of record in Project No. 58000 concerning transmission cost allocation, which bear on the
definitional recommendation in Part III.D below (Recommendations 3.E and 3.F). These comments are
organized to follow the organization of the proposed rule and address Staff’s four specific questions and
then the text of the rule itself.

I. Interest and Basis of Comments
The study of multi-utility coordination in the Port Houston Baytown-La Porte (BLP) corridor referred to
above uses exclusively public data.1 It reconstructs the corridor’s twelve-anchor industrial baseline –
approximately 7.7 TWh per year of electricity demand (90% CI [7.0, 8.4] TWh), or roughly 879 MW of
average load, within a single transmission-constrained load zone. It values coordinated, portfolio-level
cluster operation across four complementary revenue streams at a median of approximately $91.2 million
per year (P5 $64.6M; P95 $131.5M; positive in 100% of 10,000 Monte Carlo trials) against today’s
uncoordinated operation. The simulation varies the magnitude of each component and of the orchestration
cost. Because the four revenue components are individually non-negative, it bounds the size of the
coordination value rather than testing its sign.
Two quantities from that study bear directly on the questions Staff has asked, and I state them here
because the remainder of these comments depends on them. Two further quantities, the reservation price
and the empirical distribution of scarcity value, are derived in response to Question No. 2.
The corridor’s curtailable envelope is derived as follows. The study models the flexible share of corridor
load as a triangular distribution over 15%, 20%, and 25% of the 7.7 TWh baseline, calibrated to the


1
  EPA Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, reporting year 2023, facility-level data (Subparts C, P, X, Y); Texas Commission
on Environmental Quality regulated entity records for the Baytown-La Porte corridor, 2023, used to identify the anchor set
and site-level permitting; U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-923 and Form EIA-860, 2023 final release;
ERCOT Settlement Point Prices, 15-minute real-time intervals, calendar year 2023, settlement point HB_HOUSTON (35,040
intervals). Baseline figures are reconstructed from these sources alone, with stated uncertainty bands.

                                                            1
 industrial demand-flexibility literature.2 Applied to 879 MW of average load, this yields a curtailable
envelope with a central estimate of approximately 176 MW, ranging from approximately 132 MW at the
15% floor to 220 MW at the 25% ceiling, or 120 to 240 MW when the uncertainty in the demand baseline
itself is included.
The coordination value is composed as follows. The mean of that distribution, $93.7 million, decomposes
into intraday arbitrage on the Houston Hub price spread ($56.7M), four coincident peak (4CP)
transmission charge avoidance ($25.0M), ancillary service revenue ($15.0M), and imbalance avoidance
($5.0M), less $8.0M of orchestration cost. The components sum to the mean rather than to the $91.2
million median because component means are additive and medians are not; percentages of the
coordination value stated elsewhere in these comments are taken against the mean on that basis. This
decomposition matters because the eligibility conditions in proposed subsection (c)(2) do not fall on all
four components equally, as developed in response to Question No. 2.
The quantitative claims here, being the corridor baseline, the curtailable envelope, the reservation price
and the scarcity-value distribution, rest on a documented methodology built from public data, and I will
file the methodology, input distributions and workpapers in this project on Staff’s request, or provide a
technical briefing, so that the derivation can be examined rather than taken on assertion. The operational
claims, being what a facility can commit to on a given notice period, why staged multi-facility ramps are
safer than deep single-site curtailments, and what winter curtailment requires of a continuous process,
rest on two decades of work with the operators of facilities of this kind.

II. Responses to Staff’s Questions
QUESTION NO. 1: Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling
entity representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is subject
to availability verification during the LLDMS obligation period. Should a large load customer that
is available but not ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be
compensated some percentage of the market clearing price for the large load customer’s
availability to reduce demand during the LLDMS obligation period? If so, what is an appropriate
payment to the large load customer for their availability during the LLDMS obligation period?

RESPONSE:
Yes, availability should be compensated, and the payment should be mandatory rather than discretionary.
It should not, however, be expressed as a percentage of the market clearing price, for the reasons set out
in Recommendation 1.1. Staff also asks what an appropriate payment would be. I do not propose a fixed
figure and I recommend against fixing one in rule text. The appropriate payment is the price a competitive
auction clears for the availability component, subject to the floor discussed in Recommendation 1.3, and
that price cannot be known in advance because it depends on the eligibility conditions the Commission
adopts, as developed in response to Question No. 2. What can be stated is the order of magnitude the
corridor evidence implies. Where exclusivity attaches continuously, the availability price required to
reach this population is on the order of $408 per kilowatt-year; where it attaches for one obligation period
in four, on the order of $102 per kilowatt-year. Those are participants’ reservation prices rather than
proposed administered rates, and a competitive auction should clear below them.
Consider what the service is actually purchasing. The flexibility LLDMS seeks already exists behind the
fence at Texas industrial sites, built and maintained for the participants’ own commercial reasons.

2
 The 15/20/25% band is drawn from the industrial demand-flexibility literature: American Council for an Energy-Efficient
Economy, Enabling Industrial Demand Flexibility (2023); Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Demand Flexibility:
Building and Industrial Energy Systems Division Technical Brief (2022); Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Demand
Response in Industrial Facilities, ORNL/SPR-2021/2299 (2021); and Review of Industrial Load Flexibility Enhancement,
Sustainability 17(11):4938 (2025). The distribution is symmetric, so its mean, median and mode coincide at 20%.

                                                            2
 ERCOT does not need to purchase that capability. It needs to purchase a call option on it, exercisable
during defined obligation periods. On that construction, the availability payment is the option premium,
the energy payment under (f)(1)(D) is the strike, that is, the price paid on exercise, and deployment is
exercise. ERCOT obtains firm, verified demand reduction at a cost far below that of procuring equivalent
new capability, and the participant retains the production operation that justifies maintaining the
capability. What it gives up for the term of the obligation is the use of the committed megawatts for its
own account, which is the opportunity cost quantified in response to Question No. 2.
This construction is consistent with PURA § 39.170(b)(3). The statute prohibits participation by a large
load customer “that curtails in response to the wholesale price of electricity . . . or that otherwise
participates in a different reliability or ancillary service.” The operative verbs are in the present tense.
Reading the condition to attach concurrently – exclusive commitment within an obligation period,
ordinary commercial operation outside it – gives the statutory prohibition full effect while preserving the
asset that makes low-cost offers possible. No channel created by this rule compensates the same megawatt
in the same interval, and Part III.D identifies and closes the one channel outside it that otherwise would.
This reading is the one the rule should confirm, and Recommendation 3.B below asks the Commission
to do so. The construction recommended here depends on it: if eligibility under subsection (c)(2) is fixed
at an annual gate rather than assessed by obligation period, a participant cannot retain the commercial
operation that justifies maintaining the capability, and few facilities will write the option at a price the
program can afford, because each will price a full year of exclusivity into a single obligation period.
The premium, rather than the strike, is the material payment. Energy emergency alerts are infrequent. A
service deployed only during them will be exercised for a small number of hours in most years and not
at all in some, and no participant can recover the cost of a standing commitment across that many hours.
The opportunity cost of exclusivity accrues continuously through the obligation period whether or not
ERCOT deploys, while the energy payment accrues only on the hours deployed. A compensation
structure weighted toward the strike therefore asks a participant to be paid principally for an event that
may not occur. A participant will not accept nothing for the commitment; it will load the commitment
cost into its energy offer, and the offer ceiling then binds. The arithmetic is simple and does not depend
on any estimate of how often emergencies occur. At the $5,000 ceiling in (d)(3)(B)(v), an opportunity
cost of $408 per kilowatt-year can be recovered through energy alone only if the facility is deployed for
approximately 82 hours in the year, and $102 per kilowatt-year only if it is deployed for approximately
20 hours. In a year with no energy emergency alert the commitment earns nothing. Deployment-only
compensation is therefore not merely narrower; for a facility with real commitment cost it is unreachable
at the offer ceiling in all but the most severe years. Participant compensation must be recoverable
predominantly through availability, and subsections (f)(1)(C) and (D) should be structured so that it can
be, with the ratio itself left to the auction as recommended below. On the option construction set out
above this is the ordinary relationship between premium and strike, and for a service of this kind it is the
correct outcome rather than a defect to be minimized.
The objection that availability payments make the program more expensive rests on an assumption that
does not hold. It has been argued in this project that compensating only deployment keeps program costs
down, and that this is among the advantages of an as-needed rather than a seasonal design. That reasoning
holds only if the same capacity would be offered under either compensation structure. It would not be.
Deployment-only compensation prices the megawatt at the cost of the curtailment and offers nothing for
the cost of the commitment, so the loads that find it worth offering are those whose commitment cost is
near zero. The program does not become cheaper; it becomes narrower, and the population it retains will
overlap substantially with the population the Commission can already reach through the mandatory
instruments of PURA § 39.170(a) and the interconnection-stage curtailment requirements. Availability
compensation is the price of access to load that mandate cannot reach. Whether that access is worth its
cost is a question the Commission should answer directly, on the arithmetic in response to Question
No. 2, rather than by structuring the payment so that the question does not arise.

                                                     3
 Recommendation 1.1 – Do not express availability as a percentage of the market clearing price.
Under (d)(3)(A) offers are submitted in dollars per megawatt hour, and under (f)(1)(A) all payments are
based on a single clearing price. Availability, however, is an option rather than an energy delivery. Pricing
it as a fraction of a spot energy price causes availability compensation to escalate with scarcity energy
prices during periods in which no megawatt hour is delivered – an exposure with no corresponding
reliability benefit. ERCOT procures ancillary capacity on a dollars-per-megawatt basis for this reason.
The Commission should instead require a two-part offer: an availability component in dollars per
megawatt per obligation period and an energy component in dollars per megawatt hour, with a single
clearing price established for each component in the same auction. This also allows the auction rather
than the rule to determine the appropriate ratio between them. Five conforming changes follow.
Subsections (f)(1)(C) and (D) express payment as a percentage of the market clearing price and are the
provisions in which the difficulty resides; they should be reworded so that availability settles on the
availability clearing price and energy on the energy clearing price. Subsection (d)(3)(A) presently
requires offers to be expressed in dollars per megawatt hour and should be amended to accommodate a
two-part offer. Subsection (f)(1)(A) should establish a single clearing price for each component rather
than one for the service. Subsection (d)(3)(B)(v) rejects an offer greater than $5,000 per megawatt hour
and would have no application to an availability component expressed in dollars per megawatt per
obligation period, so a ceiling for that component should be supplied rather than leaving availability as
the only unpriced element of the offer. And subsection (h)(3) through (5), which require reporting of the
highest offer, the lowest offer and the cleared price, should be stated for each component.

Recommendation 1.2 – Bound the LLDMS obligation period in rule text. Proposed subsection (b)(3)
defines the term circularly, as “the period identified in a LLDMS agreement . . .” Because availability
compensation under (f)(1)(C) is keyed to that period, the rule as drafted creates an unbounded budget
exposure through an undefined term. To illustrate the magnitude: if availability were settled across the
hours of the obligation period, 500 MW procured at 25% of a $500 per megawatt hour clearing price
over a single one-month obligation period would yield approximately $45.6 million – nearly the entire
annual authorization under (f)(4), before any megawatt hour is deployed. The Commission should either
establish a maximum obligation period in rule text or specify that availability compensation settles only
on intervals in which availability is affirmatively verified. ERCOT asked for the same thing. In its
response to Commission Staff's list of questions, ERCOT stated that the rule "should specify the number
of hours a participant must be obligated to respond to one or more events or should delegate authority to
ERCOT to specify that value" (Item No. 22). Either of those mechanisms answers the exposure described
here. The proposed rule adopts neither. The exposure illustrated above grows with the length of the
obligation period, and a quarterly period on that settlement basis would be larger still. What bounds the
payment is the two-part offer recommended above, under which availability clears at auction in dollars
per megawatt per obligation period rather than as a fraction of an energy price. What quarterly obligation
periods bound, as recommended in response to Question No. 3, is the exclusivity a participant bears,
which is a different exposure and falls on the participant rather than on the budget.

Recommendation 1.3 – Retain 25% as a floor and make payment obligatory. If the Commission
retains the percentage-of-clearing-price structure, 25% is defensible as a floor once the settlement base
is corrected and should be retained as a floor while permitting availability to clear competitively above
it. If the two-part offer recommended above is adopted, the floor should be re-expressed in the availability
unit rather than as a percentage of an energy price. More consequential is the payment language itself.
The chapeau of (f)(1) provides that “ERCOT must pay a QSE that represents a large load customer
participating in LLDMS as follows,” while subparagraphs (C) and (D) provide that such a QSE “may
receive” payment. The chapeau is mandatory and the subparagraphs it introduces are permissive. The

                                                     4
 better reading is that “may receive” identifies which QSEs fall within the mandatory obligation rather
than conferring a discretion to withhold, but the question should not be left to be resolved after the fact
by a participant deciding whether to commit a plant. A participant cannot underwrite an option against a
premium that may or may not be paid, and the ambiguity buys the program nothing. The two
recommendations are sequential rather than alternative: Recommendation 1.1 changes the basis on which
subparagraphs (C) and (D) compute payment, and this recommendation changes the permissive to the
mandatory in whichever version of them the Commission adopts. Subparagraphs (C) and (D) should read
“must receive,” subject to an express exception for subsection (g), which supplies the criteria for
reducing, clawing back or suspending payment and which should govern in place of a general permissive.
The availability verification requirement already embedded in (f)(1)(C) should be retained and, if
anything, strengthened. Verification is what makes the option firm. It protects the budget against paper
commitments and it distinguishes genuine industrial capability from offers that cannot perform.
A properly structured availability payment reaches a specific population. The loads best positioned to
sell this option are the corridor anchors. They are pre-2025 interconnections, so proposed subsection
(a)(1) and PURA § 39.170(a) do not reach them, and most are expected to hold critical load industrial
customer or critical natural gas facility designations, which protect them in firm load shed on independent
grounds. For that population the availability payment is not one design detail among several. It is the
only mechanism this rule provides through which the Commission can convert existing industrial
capability into dispatchable reliability. It requires no new generation, no interconnection queue position,
no transmission construction, and no capital subsidy.

Recommendation 1.4 – Conform the cost recovery provision to the payment provision. Subsection (f)(3)
requires ERCOT to charge load serving entities for “LLDMS deployment costs,” while subsection (f)(4)
limits “procurement costs” to $54 million per calendar year. If availability payment under (f)(1)(C) is
retained, and particularly if it is made obligatory as recommended above, the rule establishes a payment
obligation with no corresponding charging authority and uses two different terms for the same
expenditure. I recommend that (f)(3) be amended to charge load serving entities for “LLDMS
procurement costs, including availability and deployment payments,” so that recovery, payment and the
budget limit describe the same thing. Subsection (f) presently uses three temporal bases for one program:
awards settle monthly under (f)(1)(B), charges are assessed “during the procurement period” under (f)(3),
and the cap runs by calendar year under (f)(4). “Procurement period” is not defined in subsection (b),
which defines only the LLDMS obligation period. The same amendment should conform that term.

QUESTION NO. 2: Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a
calendar year. What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

RESPONSE:
The budget cannot be evaluated independently of subsection (c)(2). The eligibility conditions in that
subsection determine the reservation price at which offers are submitted, and the reservation price
determines what any given budget procures. The Commission is setting one parameter, not two. The
figures that follow are computed on the reading of subsection (c)(2) under which exclusivity attaches
continuously at the facility level. I adopt that reading here not because it is the better one – Part III.B
explains why it is not – but because it is the reading a participant must price against while the question
remains open. Until the Commission confirms the timing of the eligibility test, an offer has to be priced
against the more onerous construction, and that uncertainty is itself a cost the program bears.
The arithmetic of the current draft is as follows. Subsection (d)(3)(B)(v) requires ERCOT to reject offers
above $5,000 per megawatt hour. At that ceiling, $54 million purchases 10,800 megawatt hours –
approximately 21.6 hours of deployment per calendar year at a 500 MW procurement level. That figure
assumes the entire authorization is applied to energy. It cannot be if availability is compensated at all.

                                                    5
 Availability compensation under (f)(1)(C) draws on the same budget, and at the reservation price
developed below, availability alone consumes the authorization: 132 MW at $408 per kilowatt-year
comes to approximately $54 million, leaving nothing for deployment. The two calculations are alternative
uses of one budget rather than a range. A mixed case shows the constraint plainly. If $40.8 million is
applied to availability, the program holds approximately 100 MW under obligation at any one time – and
it holds the same 100 MW whether that is 100 MW committed continuously at $408 per kilowatt-year or
400 MW enrolled and rotated quarterly at $102, since the standing obligation and its cost are the same
either way – while the remaining $13.2 million funds approximately 26 hours of deployment of that 100
MW at the offer ceiling, or approximately 264 hours at a $500 clearing price. At the offer ceiling that is
about one day, against a February 2021 event that persisted for several; at a lower clearing price it is a
great deal more. The hours therefore turn entirely on where energy clears. The megawatts do not: on the
rule as drafted the program can hold on the order of 100 to 132 MW of demand reduction under obligation
statewide, and every dollar reserved for the energy payment reduces that figure further. The budget is
adequate or grossly inadequate depending entirely on where offers clear.
Where offers clear is determined by opportunity cost. A facility offering into LLDMS prices its offer not
at the marginal cost of curtailment but at the opportunity cost of what it must forgo, and the corridor
study’s component decomposition makes that quantity calculable. Two of the four components are
foreclosed by a commitment to this service, on different grounds. Proposed subsection (c)(2)(B),
implementing PURA § 39.170(b)(3), bars a participant from ancillary services for the period of its
eligibility, which forecloses the ancillary services component ($15.0M). The intraday arbitrage
component ($56.7M) is foreclosed by the commitment itself rather than by an eligibility condition: a
megawatt sold to ERCOT as an availability option for an obligation period cannot at the same time be
shifted between hours for the participant’s own account. Together these are $71.7 million of forgone
annual value. One qualification should be stated plainly. The component figures come from a study that
values coordinated portfolio operation against today’s uncoordinated operation, so $56.7 million is the
value of coordinated intraday arbitrage rather than of what a facility earns operating alone today. That is
the correct counterfactual for a portfolio, because coordinated arbitrage and an ERCOT availability
option are alternative uses of the same megawatt once the portfolio exists; for a facility offering alone it
overstates the opportunity cost. The reservation price developed below should accordingly be read as an
order of magnitude rather than a point estimate, and the conclusion it supports – that the eligibility
conditions rather than the appropriation determine what the budget buys – does not depend on the exact
figure. The 4CP avoidance and imbalance components are foreclosed by neither and, on the definitional
recommendation in Part III.D below (Recommendation 3.F), would be retained.
Dividing forgone value by the corridor’s curtailable envelope of approximately 176 MW yields a
reservation price of approximately $408 per kilowatt-year where exclusivity attaches continuously at the
facility level. Applying the same budget:
•     At $408/kW-yr, the entire $54 million statewide authorization procures approximately 132 MW of
      demand reduction statewide, and would leave nothing for the energy payment subsection (f)(1)(D)
      provides for on deployment.
•     Under quarterly obligation periods, whether or not participants are aggregated, a given facility bears
      exclusivity for one period in four rather than continuously, and the burden it prices into its offer falls
      accordingly. Two consequences follow and they should not be confused. The same authorization
      enrolls a substantially larger body of qualified capability, on the order of 530 MW rather than 132
      MW, because the commitment asked of each participant is smaller. It does not by itself increase the
      demand reduction callable at any single moment: with roughly a quarter of the enrolled capability
      under obligation in any given period, the megawatts available to ERCOT during a particular
      emergency remain set by the budget. The gain lies in the depth, diversity and seasonal fit of the pool
      from which each period’s obligation is drawn, and more consequentially in the size of the population



                                                       6
       willing to offer at all. That accounting holds at a fixed clearing price. The clearing price, however,
      is not fixed.
      That last point is where the budget arithmetic turns. A program able to reach only those loads
      prepared to bear continuous exclusivity is bidding against a short and steep supply curve. Most
      industrial facilities will decline that commitment at any price this program can pay, not because the
      capability is absent but because a year of exclusivity is indivisible from a year of production
      scheduling. Reducing the commitment to a single obligation period brings a materially larger
      population within reach, and the price a competitive auction clears from a deep supply curve is lower
      than the price it clears from a shallow one. The Commission should expect aggregated participation
      to procure more demand reduction per dollar than the site-by-site case, and should expect that
      difference to be realized through the clearing price rather than through any arithmetic division of
      the reservation price. One consequence of subsection (f)(1)(A) belongs here as well. All payments
      are based on a single clearing price, so the marginal offer sets the price for every participant. An
      auction opened without regard to the character of the flexibility offered will clear against whatever
      load can commit at the lowest cost, and the megawatt total may look satisfactory while the industrial
      process load this service is best placed to reach does not clear at all. That is a further reason for the
      two-part offer recommended in response to Question No. 1, which lets the auction price the
      commitment rather than the energy, and for the pre-qualification reporting recommended below,
      without which the Commission cannot see who offered and who did not.
Three qualifications attach to these figures, and they do not all run the same way. Assuming that offers
recover the whole of forgone value overstates the price and therefore understates procurable capacity.
Assuming that the entire authorization is applied to availability overstates capacity, because subsection
(f)(1)(D) provides for an energy payment on deployment and whatever share is reserved for it reduces
what the availability payment can procure; $54 million at $408 per kilowatt-year is approximately 132
MW, which absorbs essentially the whole authorization. And the reservation price is computed by
dividing value captured by the participating share of the corridor by the corridor’s full physical envelope,
which understates the opportunity cost borne per participating kilowatt. The second and third effects
dominate, so 132 MW should be read as the most favorable figure available to the current draft rather
than as an estimate of what it will deliver. That is what makes the first result significant: on the rule as
drafted, the entire statewide annual budget procures less demand reduction than a single industrial
corridor is physically capable of providing. I state the relationship precisely, because it is arithmetic rather
than coincidence. The 132 MW procurable statewide is 176 MW multiplied by the ratio of the $54 million
authorization to the $71.7 million of forgone value, so it is roughly three-quarters of 176 MW for the
same reason that $54 million is roughly three-quarters of $71.7 million. The translation from dollars into
megawatts is the point rather than a second finding: for a reliability service the question before the
Commission is physical, and the physical statement is that the entire statewide authorization buys less
than one corridor holds. A separate coincidence should be noted so that it is not mistaken for
corroboration. Approximately 132 MW is also the 15% floor of the corridor’s curtailable envelope (0.15
× 879 MW). That figure and the procurement figure are derived independently, and their agreement
carries no significance.
Stated the other way, the two channels a participant must forgo in order to serve this obligation are worth
approximately $71.7 million per year to this corridor alone – roughly a third more than the entire $54
million annual statewide budget the Commission proposes to spend on the service. The two are not
commensurable as pools of money: one is private opportunity cost borne by participants, the other a
program budget recovered from load serving entities. The comparison is offered to establish scale. The
participation decision the rule asks of a single industrial corridor is larger than the program itself.
The ratio between the two procurement figures, approximately four to one, does not depend on the
absolute level of opportunity cost and holds whatever the true reservation price proves to be. It does,
however, follow from the quarterly obligation period recommended in response to Question No. 3: the

                                                       7
 Commission’s choice of obligation period sets the rotation interval and therefore the ratio. A shorter
period would widen it and a longer one would narrow it. Two qualifications attach. The ratio describes
enrolled capability rather than capability under obligation at a given moment, as set out above. And it
treats the burden of exclusivity as uniform across the year, which the empirical record does not support:
as the daily spread distribution set out under Recommendation 2.1 shows, scarcity value at the Houston
hub is concentrated in a small number of days. A facility bearing exclusivity through a summer obligation
period forgoes more than one quarter of annual value and one bearing it in spring forgoes less.
Participants will price accordingly, and a portfolio will pay a premium to cover the periods of greatest
system need. A further qualification follows from the same point. If procurement concentrates in the
seasons of greatest risk, there is no inexpensive shoulder period to rotate into, and rotation within a year
delivers less than the ratio implies; the durable form of the effect is rotation of a given season’s obligation
among portfolio members across years. The four-to-one figure should therefore be read as the outer bound
of the effect rather than as a forecast.
Whether the eligible population exists. It has been suggested in this project that the service should target
loads that, by their nature, do not actively participate in the market, on the premise that flexible load is
already reached by existing instruments. The evidence does not support that premise. The Houston
Energy Transition Initiative, which convenes policymakers, generation, transmission and distribution
utilities and ratepayer interests within the Greater Houston Partnership, published an assessment of
efficiency and demand response on August 7, 2026. It reports the registered non-controllable load
resource pool in ERCOT growing from approximately 3,500 MW in 2018 to more than 10,000 MW,
while ancillary market clears from that pool remain between 1,800 and 2,500 MW. It names as latent
flexible load those customers not registered as demand response resources that could modify operations
under appropriate commercial, regulatory or market structures, and identifies broad aggregation models
and large-load flexibility arrangements as lacking a clear pathway under current ERCOT and
Commission rules.
A corridor anchor has described the same condition from the inside. In Project No. 58000, Occidental
Chemical Corporation states that its co-located sites “have the flexibility to reduce their co-located load
in order to increase exports, which provides additional dispatchable capacity on the grid at critical times,”
while also explaining that integrated cogeneration facilities “generally cannot treat electric load reduction
as a simple economic response without potentially disrupting production, process safety, product quality,
contractual commitments, or steam system reliability.” Both statements are correct, and together they
describe precisely the population this service should reach: capability that exists, is dispatchable, and
cannot be summoned by a price signal. That is the case for structuring LLDMS as an availability option
on existing capability, as recommended in response to Question No. 1, rather than as a price-responsive
product. I note that the same commenter supports retaining the 4CP methodology and does not treat
coincident peak avoidance as a primary operational objective, which bears on the component discussed
in Part III.D below.
Two populations are described and they should not be merged. The first is registered: the gap between
more than 10,000 MW of registered non-controllable load resource capability and 1,800 to 2,500 MW of
ancillary clears is capability that is qualified and not delivering. A customer that is registered but not
clearing in a given period is not, in that period, a customer that otherwise participates in an ancillary
service, and is therefore eligible on the reading of subsection (c)(2) developed in Part III.B. The second

 QUESTION NO. 3: What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and
how far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

RESPONSE:
The proposed rule establishes two of the three clocks this service requires, and the third is the subject of
this question. Subsection (c) sets the qualification clock, requiring pre-qualification at least annually.
Subsection (e)(1) sets the deployment clock, requiring at least 24 hours’ notice. The procurement lead
time – the interval between the close of the auction and the start of the obligation period – is not specified
anywhere in the draft.
These are not interchangeable. Twenty-four hours is sufficient for an industrial facility to execute a
curtailment it has already planned for: to sequence a staged turndown, notify downstream customers
under existing contractual provisions, and position operating staff. It is not sufficient for that facility to
determine whether such a curtailment is feasible at all. That determination depends on batch campaign
scheduling, turnaround windows, feedstock and product logistics, and firm delivery obligations
committed weeks to months in advance. A facility asked at short notice whether it can shed 40 MW next
week will decline – not because the flexibility does not exist, but because the analysis and the contractual
accommodation cannot be completed in the interval offered.
Lead time is a price lever, and the least expensive one available to the Commission. For an industrial
process load the cost of a committed demand reduction falls into three regimes distinguished only by
notice. Procured 30 days or more ahead, the facility re-sequences production around the obligation –
shifting campaigns, adjusting intermediate inventories, re-timing maintenance – and the cost is the
efficiency loss from operating away from its unconstrained optimum. Procured at 24 hours to one week,
the facility must reduce throughput against a fixed schedule, and the cost is forgone production margin.
Procured intra-event under (d)(1)(D), the facility curtails from a running state with restart costs and, in
continuous processes, off-specification product. These are the most expensive megawatts the program
will buy.
The corridor study bears on this in two distinct ways that should not be conflated. First, it establishes that
the capability exists and is commercially valuable: the modeled coordination value is generated by
flexibility the corridor already operates. That is the basis for treating LLDMS as an option on an existing
asset rather than a purchase of a new one. Second, and separately, forward procurement determines
whether that capability is available in the obligation window at low cost. Intraday flexibility operates on
a within-day horizon and does not itself require thirty days’ notice; what requires forward notice is
production scheduling. A facility given a month can position its campaign plan so that slack exists during
the obligation period. A facility called at 24 hours may find the window occupied by a firm delivery
commitment.

Recommendation 3.1 – Retain monthly probabilistic assessment and anchor it to the seasonal cycle.
The monthly probabilistic modeling contemplated by subsection (d)(1)(A) is the correct primary
instrument. The Commission should require that it be anchored to ERCOT’s existing seasonal resource
adequacy assessment cycle and updated on a rolling monthly basis, so that the risk signal driving
procurement is continuous rather than episodic.

Recommendation 3.2 – Require ERCOT to publish the forward risk signal at the same monthly
cadence. Information costs the program nothing and lowers offers: a participant able to observe the same
forward signal ERCOT is acting on can pre-position its production schedule rather than pricing that
uncertainty into its offer.

Recommendation 3.3 – Establish a two-tranche procurement structure. A planned tranche, procured
on the (d)(1)(A) monthly signal, with the auction closing not less than 30 days before the start of the

                                                     11
 obligation period. This is the tranche accessible to industrial process loads, and because it is procured
against a forward rather than an imminent risk signal it should clear materially below short-lead
procurement. Staff asks how far in advance ERCOT should start the auction. For the planned tranche I
recommend that ERCOT issue the request for proposal not less than 60 days, and close the auction not
less than 30 days, before the start of the obligation period. The interval between issuance and close is
what allows a process load to complete the internal analysis and contractual accommodation described
above; the interval between close and the obligation period is what allows it to position its production
schedule against a commitment it has won. The planning value of forward procurement is not a
proposition ERCOT disputes. Comparing the two designs Staff put to it, ERCOT observed that under an
as-needed approach it "would not know the amount of demand response capability procured until a few
days before the event," whereas knowing the quantity further ahead lets ERCOT "better use that
information in its advance planning," with "more flexibility to use that procurement to address non-storm
related Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) events or transmission emergencies" (Item No. 22). The
Commission adopted the as-needed design. A planned tranche recovers the advance-planning benefit
ERCOT identified without displacing that choice. A contingency tranche should retain the (d)(1)(B)
through (D) triggers for risk that materializes inside the planning window. The Commission should
recognize that this tranche will clear at a substantial premium and limit it to a defined minority share of
the annual budget; no more than 40% is a reasonable starting parameter.

Recommendation 3.4 – Define obligation periods on a quarterly basis aligned to ERCOT’s seasonal
assessment cycle. This bounds the availability exposure identified in response to Question No. 1 and
establishes the natural rotation interval for aggregated portfolios.

Recommendation 3.5 – Permit standing offers spanning multiple consecutive obligation periods, so
that a qualified facility or portfolio may offer once against a rolling forward horizon rather than re-bidding
each cycle. Repeated bidding is an administrative cost that falls disproportionately on process loads with
long internal approval chains, and it is a cost the program need not impose.
This structure does not revisit the Commission’s choice of an as-needed rather than a seasonal service. It
implements subsection (d)(1)(A) with the lead time that provision’s own monthly modeling horizon
already implies, and it preserves the responsiveness that motivated the as-needed design.
There is a further benefit. Short-notice procurement can only buy flexibility that already exists. A facility
that knows in March it may be called in August can make modest scheduling and capital accommodations
– intermediate storage, batch sequencing, dual-feed arrangements – that enlarge what it is able to offer.
This effect will not appear in the first procurement cycle and should not be expected to. It is nonetheless
the principal reason to establish the forward tranche in rule text rather than leaving lead time to protocol
development.

QUESTION NO. 4: Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies?
If so, what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

RESPONSE:
Yes. I note at the outset that the defined term “transmission emergency” in proposed subsection (b)(4)
appears nowhere in the operative provisions of the rule. Subsections (d) and (e) key procurement and
deployment exclusively to an EEA event arising from an extreme weather condition. As drafted, the
definition is without effect.
The statutory case is straightforward. PURA § 39.170(b) directs the Commission to require ERCOT to
develop a reliability service to competitively procure demand reductions “to be deployed in the event of
an anticipated emergency condition.” That phrase is not confined to extreme weather. The Legislature
used the same phrase in the adjacent section of the same act. PURA § 39.169 requires that conditions on

                                                     12
 a net metering arrangement direct an existing generation resource to make dispatchable capacity available
“in advance of an anticipated emergency condition,” and nothing in that section confines the phrase to
extreme weather. The Commission adopted that language into § 25.205(k)(1) of this title on March 26,
2026 without a weather qualifier. The same words in § 39.170(b) should carry the same meaning.
Subsection (b)(1) requires the governing rules to “specify the periods when the service may be used to
assist with maintaining reliability during extreme weather events.” It has been suggested that this
language confines deployment to extreme weather events. That reading cannot be reconciled with the
structure of the subsection or with the Commission’s own treatment of it.
Section 39.170(b) grants the deployment authority in its chapeau and then imposes three mandatory
content requirements on the rules: (b)(1) on periods of use, (b)(2) on notice and duration, and (b)(3) on
eligibility prohibitions. Each specifies something the rules must contain. None purports to describe the
outer limit of the authority the chapeau confers. Reading (b)(1) as a ceiling requires reading the parallel
paragraphs the same way – and the Commission has not done so. Proposed subsection (c)(2) adds six
grounds of ineligibility beyond the three in (b)(3), which is defensible only if (b)(3) states a minimum
rather than an exhaustive list. Reading (b)(3) as a floor and (b)(1) as a ceiling would give the same
drafting convention two different effects within one subsection. If the paragraphs are minimum content
requirements, as the drafting of (c)(2) assumes, then the deployment authority is the one the chapeau
grants: an anticipated emergency condition.
A transmission emergency as the Commission has itself defined it in proposed (b)(4) – an element
operating above its emergency rating such that it creates a significant risk of firm load shed – is an
anticipated emergency condition on an ordinary reading. ERCOT has read the statute the same way.
Asked by Commission Staff whether PURA authorizes deployment in circumstances other than extreme
weather events, ERCOT answered that the language "does not say that the service is to be deployed in
the event of an 'anticipated extreme weather event.'" It concluded that "a plain language reading of the
statute gives the Commission authority to draft a broader rule to address circumstances that are unrelated
to an extreme weather event, including an anticipated EEA event, transmission emergency, or other
emergency condition that may not be associated with extreme weather" (Item No. 22). The operator of
the service has told the Commission that the broader construction is available to it. Confining deployment
to weather-driven EEA events forgoes authority the Legislature granted, and does so in precisely the
circumstance where the demand reduction procured is most precisely targeted.
The operational case rests on locational value. An EEA is a system-wide energy shortfall, and demand
reduction anywhere in the ERCOT region contributes to resolving it. A transmission emergency is a
constraint on a specific element, and only demand reduction electrically behind that constraint
contributes. Co-located industrial concentrations are by construction the resources best positioned to
provide it: the BLP corridor represents approximately 879 MW of average industrial demand within a
single load zone. This is also the circumstance in which aggregated participation is most valuable,
because a coordinated portfolio can deliver a locationally precise block behind an identified constraint,
whereas individual site offers cannot be assembled into one on the timescale a transmission emergency
allows.

Recommendation 4.1 – Supply the operative provisions, and limit deployment to constraints
identified in advance. The recommendations that follow presuppose an amendment the proposed rule
does not contain. The chapeau of subsection (d) authorizes procurement only to prevent an anticipated
EEA event or alleviate an actual EEA event due to an extreme weather condition, and subsections (e)(2)
and (e)(3)(A) key deployment and its duration to the same event, so the definition at (b)(4) has nothing
to operate on. The Commission should extend the subsection (d) chapeau, each of the request-for-
proposal triggers in (d)(1), and subsection (e)(2) to an anticipated transmission emergency, and should
supply a corresponding endpoint in (e)(3). Because a deployment made in advance may prevent the
condition from arising at all, that endpoint should be the period ERCOT specifies in the deployment

                                                    13
 instruction rather than the duration of a condition that may never occur, and Recommendation 4.4 should
be read accordingly. The service contemplated here is deployment in advance of a transmission
emergency rather than a response to one already in progress: an element operating above its emergency
rating is a condition measured in minutes, and a 24-hour instrument can be used to prevent that condition,
not to relieve it. Deployment should then be limited to constraints identified in advance in a posted
ERCOT transmission assessment or equivalent study, rather than on an ad hoc operational determination.
This confines the authority to conditions ERCOT has analyzed and disclosed, and gives potential
participants the forward information they need in order to offer.

Recommendation 4.2 – Impose a sub-cap within the annual budget. Locational procurement
addresses a narrower reliability need than system-wide emergency response and should not consume the
budget available for the latter; ten percent of the annual authorization is a reasonable starting parameter.
Three budget partitions are recommended in these comments and they should be given a single order of
precedence. Deployments under (d)(1)(D) during an actual EEA event should be excluded from the cap
under Recommendation 2.2; the contingency tranche under Recommendation 3.3 should be limited to
40% of the remaining authorization; and transmission-emergency procurement should be limited to 10%
of it. If the Commission declines Recommendation 2.2, deployments under (d)(1)(D) fall inside the
contingency tranche and are subject to its limit.

Recommendation 4.3 – Apply the 24-hour notice requirement without modification. The 24-hour
notice derives from PURA § 39.170(b)(2). Transmission emergencies can develop rapidly and there will
be pressure to shorten notice for this deployment class, but a shortened window would exclude precisely
the industrial loads whose locational position makes them valuable here, leaving the authority useful only
against loads already curtailable by other means.

Recommendation 4.4 – Specify the duration obligation. PURA § 39.170(b)(2) requires a deployed
load to remain curtailed “for the duration of the energy emergency alert event or until the load can be
recalled safely.” A transmission emergency will not involve an EEA, so the rule must supply an
analogous endpoint – the duration of the identified constraint condition, or until ERCOT determines the
load can be recalled safely.

Recommendation 4.5 – Extend after-action reporting under subsection (h) to transmission-emergency
deployments, with the report additionally identifying the specific constraint relieved and the megawatt
quantity deployed behind it.

Recommendation 4.6 – Sunset the authority for a given constraint once a transmission solution
addressing that constraint is energized. Procured demand reduction is a reasonable bridge to a
transmission upgrade. It is not a substitute for one, and a standing authority to deploy it against a known
constraint would weaken the case for building the upgrade. A constraint-specific sunset preserves the
reliability benefit while keeping the incentive to solve the underlying problem intact.

III. Comments on the Text of the Proposed Rule
The recommendations in this Part concern a single subject: the participation of more than one qualifying
large load customer in the service through a common qualified scheduling entity. I begin with two
observations that frame what is actually being asked.
The proposed rule already presumes a representative entity. Offers are submitted by a QSE under
(d)(3)(A); deployment notice is given to a QSE under (e)(1); payment is made to a QSE under (f)(1); and
payment reduction, clawback and suspension attach to a QSE under (g)(1). Qualification under


                                                    14
 subsection (c), deployment under (e)(2) and (e)(3), and suspension under (g)(2) attach to the large load
customer. The rule therefore already separates the entity that transacts with the program from the entity
that performs. That separation is the architecture of a portfolio offer, and the proposed rule contains every
element of it except permission to place more than one customer behind the transacting entity. The QSE
is already the aggregating entity in this design. It is simply, at present, an entity that aggregates a portfolio
of one.
Nothing in the statute or the rule prohibits a QSE from representing more than one qualifying customer.
PURA § 39.170 does not address the question, and neither does the text of the proposed rule: the words
“aggregate” and “portfolio” appear nowhere in it. The Commission has, however, already written the
provision that is missing here. Under § 25.507(d)(2)(B) of this title, QSEs representing Emergency
Response Service resources “may aggregate multiple loads to reach the minimum capacity offer
requirement established by ERCOT,” and such aggregations “will be considered a single ERS resource
for purposes of submitting offers.” Multi-load representation behind a single QSE is not a novel construct
in Commission rules. It is an established one, adopted for the Commission’s existing emergency demand
response program. Staff’s memorandum accompanying this proposal describes a design in which a QSE
“may submit offers on behalf of an individual load.” That describes the case Staff had in view. It is not a
determination that a QSE may not represent two, and neither the preamble nor the memorandum offers a
reason why portfolio representation would be inconsistent with the statute or with reliability. The
ordinary rule of construction points the same way. Subsection (d)(3)(A) requires a QSE to submit an
offer “on behalf of a large load customer,” and under Texas Government Code § 311.012(b) the singular
includes the plural. Nothing requires that provision to be read as confining a QSE to one customer, and
nothing else in the rule does so. Portfolio participation is therefore not prohibited by the proposed rule;
it is unprovided for.
Accordingly the recommendations below are offered in three tiers, in ascending order of what they ask
of the Commission. The first conforms the rule to the statutory grant and requires no new policy. The
second confirms the timing of an eligibility test the rule already contains. The third would provide
affirmatively for portfolio participation and is the only one that adds structure. The order is also one of
dependency. Tier two determines whether exclusivity under subsection (c)(2) is perpetual or periodic,
and that question governs the price at which any participant can offer, aggregated or not. Tier one
determines whether a customer whose qualifying demand is distributed across adjacent sites falls within
the definition at all. Without those two, the third has little to operate on. The Commission may adopt the
first two without reaching the third.

A. Tier one – conform subsection (b)(2) to the statutory grant
PURA § 39.170(b) directs ERCOT to procure demand reductions "from large load customers with a
demand of at least 75 megawatts." The statute sets the 75 MW threshold, and I do not propose to disturb
it. It does not require that the threshold be satisfied at a single location, and the omission is not an accident
of drafting. Senate Bill 6 added PURA § 39.169 and § 39.170 by the same section of the bill, and in §
39.169 the Legislature reached the interconnection class expressly, requiring notice before implementing
a net metering arrangement between a registered stand-alone generation resource and "a new large load
customer as described by Section 37.0561(c)." Where the drafter wanted the § 37.0561(c) class in Chapter
39, it said so in those words. In § 39.170(b), enacted by the same section of the same bill, it did not. The
proposed rule itself depends on that incorporation, because subsection (c)(2)(F) ties eligibility to a net
metering arrangement under PURA § 39.169, which is defined by reference to § 37.0561(c). The
Commission is construing a term the Legislature anchored to § 37.0561(c) once, deliberately, and left
unanchored in the provision this rulemaking implements.
That § 37.0561(c) is not itself a definition of the customer class reinforces the point. It states when the
interconnection standards apply: they "must apply only to customers requesting a new or expanded
interconnection where the total load at a single site would exceed a demand threshold established by the

                                                       15
 commission based on the size of loads that significantly impact transmission needs in the ERCOT power
region," and the Commission is directed to set that threshold at 75 megawatts "unless the commission
determines that a lower threshold is necessary." The number there is a Commission-established default
that may be adjusted downward; the number in § 39.170(b) is fixed by the Legislature. Section 37.0561(a)
confines its own usage in the same way, providing that "[f]or the purposes of this section, a large load
customer includes an entity requesting an interconnection that exceeds the demand threshold adopted
under Subsection (c)" – a formulation that is inclusive rather than exhaustive and that does not reach
beyond its own section.
There is also a reason of function why the Commission should not supply the qualifier itself. Section
37.0561 governs interconnection. It asks what transmission infrastructure a new or expanded connection
at a physical point requires, and for that question a single-site test is the right test. Section 39.170(b)
governs the competitive procurement of demand reductions from customers, which is a commercial
question about who may sell curtailment rather than a physical question about what must be built. A test
written for the first question does not answer the second.
Proposed subsection (b)(2) defines a large load customer as “[a]n entity with a total non-coincident peak
demand at a single site that is equal to or greater than 75 megawatts.” The words “at a single site” have
no counterpart in § 39.170. They have a counterpart in § 37.0561(c), which governs a different instrument
and applies only to customers requesting a new or expanded interconnection. The corridor’s anchor
facilities are neither. The qualifier appears once in the thirteen pages of the proposal, in the definition
itself, and is not explained in the preamble, in the statement of statutory authority, or in Staff’s
memorandum recommending publication. Staff’s own presentation in this project states the participation
criterion as loads of 75 MW or greater, without the qualifier. Its effect is that a customer whose total
demand across several facilities within one industrial corridor exceeds 75 MW – and which therefore
satisfies the statutory threshold on the statute’s own terms – is nonetheless excluded from the program.
This pattern is present in the BLP corridor. Texas Commission on Environmental Quality regulated entity
records for 2023 identify more than a dozen operators holding two or more separately permitted sites
within the corridor, the largest holding fourteen. Those records establish common ownership and
adjacency rather than electrical demand, and I do not assert that any particular operator would qualify on
amendment; the point is only that the configuration the qualifier excludes is common rather than
exceptional.

Recommendation 3.A – Amend subsection (b)(2) to read "a total non-coincident peak demand at a single
site, or a combined demand across multiple sites of the same customer located within a single ERCOT
load zone measured in the same 15-minute settlement interval, that is equal to or greater than 75
megawatts," or in the alternative strike "at a single site." Either form conforms the rule to the statutory
grant. Neither lowers the 75 MW threshold and neither permits a sub-threshold customer to participate.
I recommend the amended form rather than the bare strike, because the load zone qualifier preserves a
locational limit on the face of the definition and complements the narrower contiguity requirement
recommended in Part III.C. The measurement basis is deliberate. Peaks at different sites do not occur at
the same time, and a rule that simply summed them would admit a customer that never presents 75
megawatts to the system. Requiring the multi-site total to be reached within a single settlement interval
holds the threshold where the Legislature set it. I avoid the term "coincident peak" for this purpose,
because elsewhere in this rulemaking and in Project No. 58000 it denotes the transmission cost allocation
construct, which is a different measurement made for a different purpose. If the Commission prefers the
bare strike, it should supply the same measurement rule by protocol. The Commission may of course
conclude that a single-site test serves the purposes of this service. If it does, the basis should be stated on
the record, because the Legislature wrote such a test into § 37.0561(c) and did not write one into §
39.170(b).

 B. Tier two – confirm the timing of the eligibility test under subsection (c)(2)
The provision that determines whether portfolio participation is economically possible is the timing of

C. Tier three – provide affirmatively for an aggregated resource
The two recommendations above make portfolio participation workable. The recommendations in this
section would make it administrable and repeatable, and I offer them as the third and largest tier.
I state the case for it in the order in which the benefits bear on the Commission’s mandate, rather than in
the order in which they accrue.
The first benefit accrues to the program and to ratepayers. The arithmetic is set out in response to Question
No. 2 and I do not repeat it, except to identify what is at stake. Where exclusivity attaches continuously
at the facility level, the population able to offer is narrow and the authorization procures on the order of
132 MW of demand reduction statewide. Where a portfolio can distribute the commitment among
qualifying members across obligation periods, the same authorization reaches a qualified pool several
times that size and clears against a deeper supply curve. The megawatts ERCOT can call at any one
moment are the authorized spend divided by the clearing price. Portfolio participation does not change
the spend; it lowers the price at which the marginal megawatt clears and widens the qualified population
that price is drawn from, so the same sum buys reliability of better composition and, at the margin, more
of it. That difference is not a benefit conferred on participants. It is reliability the Commission either does
or does not obtain for a fixed sum recovered from load serving entities. Of the changes that would add
text to this rule, portfolio participation is the least expensive per unit of reliability purchased.
The second accrues to the reliability of the ERCOT system. Two operational properties follow from
portfolio measurement, and neither can be relied on from individual site offers, where the locational
composition of what is procured is whatever the offers that happen to arrive produce. A portfolio can
deliver a locationally precise block behind an identified constraint, which is what makes the transmission-
emergency authority discussed in response to Question No. 4 useful rather than nominal. And staged
turndowns sequenced across several facilities are operationally safer for integrated complexes than
isolated deep curtailments at a single site, because the deliverable envelope is assembled from shallow
reductions at many points rather than a severe reduction at one.
The third accrues to participants. A facility that bears exclusivity for one obligation period in four rather
than continuously can offer at a materially lower price. This is a benefit to participants only in the sense
that it makes participation possible; its consequence for the Commission is the reservation price, which
is a cost to the program.

F. Responses to comments of record
The recommendations above are offered on their own terms. Four matters raised by other commenters in
this project bear on them directly, and I address those here rather than leave them implicit.
Locational integrity of curtailment. Oncor has recommended that curtailment responsibility be allocated
solely to the large loads that ERCOT dispatches, that the QSE of a participating large load not be
permitted to transfer a curtailment obligation to other participating loads in its portfolio, and that load
reduction be location and load specific, on the ground that allocating or transferring obligations from one



                                                    21
 load to another in a different geographic area could frustrate ERCOT’s ability to respond to localized
emergency conditions (Item No. 18).
I accept that principle, and Recommendation 3.C is drawn to give effect to it. Oncor’s concern has two
parts and both are met. The first is substitution: that a dispatched load’s obligation might be discharged
by another load in the same portfolio. Rotation as recommended here is not substitution. It is assignment,
made at procurement and fixed before the obligation period opens. Within an obligation period each
member’s committed quantity is fixed, individually metered and separately measured; a shortfall by one
member is not cured by over-delivery by another. The portfolio baseline is a means of measuring
individually committed quantities in aggregate, not a means of exchanging them. The second is
geography: that an obligation might move to a facility in a different area. The structure recommended
here does not permit it. Portfolio membership is confined to facilities within a contiguous industrial area
or served by common transmission infrastructure and, in all cases, within a single ERCOT load zone. An
obligation assigned among the twelve anchor facilities of the Baytown-La Porte corridor does not move
between geographic areas. It moves within a contiguous industrial concentration served by common
transmission infrastructure. The load zone requirement is an outer bound that makes the limit
administrable in settlement; it is the contiguity requirement that keeps the obligation behind the same
constraints, and I do not suggest that a load zone is itself a constraint boundary.
The locational consideration runs the other way. As set out in response to Question No. 4, a co-located
portfolio is the only structure capable of delivering a locationally precise block of demand reduction
behind an identified transmission constraint on the timescale a transmission emergency allows; individual
site offers cannot be assembled into such a block after the constraint appears. If locational specificity is
a requirement of this service rather than an inconvenience, that is a reason to provide for portfolio
participation within a defined area rather than to withhold it. Recommendation 3.C so provides, and
Recommendation 3.A carries the same limit into the definition itself.
Eligibility drawn around configuration rather than capability. Several commenters have urged that the
participation framework not exclude dispatchable capability by reason of the configuration in which it is
held (Item Nos. 14, 20, 24 and 25). Those comments concern generation co-located with a single load.
The recommendation here concerns load co-located with load. The structural point is common to both:
eligibility drawn around the configuration in which capability is held, rather than around the capability
itself, excludes reliability that the service exists to procure. I take no position on the merits of the co-
located generation arguments, which raise questions under PURA § 37.0561(e) and § 39.169 that are not
presented here; the latter governed by § 25.205 of this title.
Qualification and verification. ERCOT has recommended that each participant be required to attest that
it can safely ramp down within twenty-four hours, noting that ERCOT does not have an independent
means of confirming ramp capability at the qualification stage (Item No. 22). Portfolio participation
offers a practical answer to that difficulty. Where several facilities are represented together, capability
can be demonstrated through a coordinated test deployment measured at the portfolio level, which
substitutes observation for attestation without imposing a site-by-site testing obligation that ERCOT
would otherwise have to administer. Recommendation 3.D is drafted with that in mind.
Program evaluation. Modern Tex Consulting has proposed adding paragraphs (9) through (14) to
subsection (h), covering total program expenditures, participants by procurement period, availability
performance, deployment frequency and duration, cost per megawatt procured, and cost-effectiveness
comparisons (Item No. 34). I support those additions. I note only that neither subsection (h) as proposed
nor the additions proposed there would show how many large load customers sought pre-qualification
and were found ineligible. Modern Tex’s proposed paragraph (10) counts participants. Recommendation
2.5 counts applicants, and the difference between the two is the only direct measure of whether the
eligibility conditions in subsection (c)(2) are constraining supply.
